Write JavaScript that adds a 'submit' event listener to the form with id 'name-form'. The handler should: (1) call e.preventDefault(), (2) get the value from the input with id 'name-input', (3) use createElement to create a new <li> with textContent set to the input value, (4) appendChild the <li> to the <ul> with id 'name-list', (5) clear the input value after adding.
What does `e.preventDefault()` do, and why is it essential when handling a form 'submit' event? What would happen without it?
questions.sample_answer: `e.preventDefault()` stops the browser's default action for that event. For a form submit, the default action is to send an HTTP request to the server and reload the page. Without it, the page refreshes immediately after the user clicks submit, so any JavaScript that runs after the submit (like adding items to a list or showing a message) would be lost because the page reloads and resets to its initial state. By calling preventDefault, we keep the page intact and handle the form data entirely with JavaScript.

When the user presses the 'Enter' key (check e.key === 'Enter'), set the textContent of the element with id 'result' to 'Searching for: ' followed by the input's value. When the user presses 'Escape', clear both the input value and the result textContent.

Write JavaScript that: (1) uses createElement to create a new <div> with class 'card' and textContent 'New Card', (2) creates a <button> with textContent '×' and class 'delete-btn', (3) adds a click event listener to the button that calls remove() on its parent element, (4) appends the button to the div, then appends the div to the element with id 'container'.
What is the difference between `e.target` and `e.currentTarget` in an event handler? Give a scenario where they would be different.
questions.sample_answer: `e.target` is the element that actually triggered the event — the element the user interacted with directly. `e.currentTarget` is the element that the event listener is attached to. They differ when events bubble. Scenario: a <ul> has a click listener. The user clicks a <span> inside an <li>. `e.target` is the <span> (what was clicked), while `e.currentTarget` is the <ul> (where the listener lives). This is the basis of event delegation — you attach one listener to a parent and use e.target to determine which child was clicked.

Write JavaScript that adds an 'input' event listener to the text input with id 'char-input'. On each keystroke, update the textContent of the element with id 'char-count' to show the current length of the input's value (e.g., '5 characters'). If the length exceeds 20, add class 'warning' to the counter; otherwise remove it.
Explain the difference between the 'input' event and the 'keydown' event on a text input. When would you choose one over the other?
questions.sample_answer: The 'input' event fires after the input's value has already changed — you always get the updated value. It fires for any value change: typing, pasting, autocomplete, cutting, or speech input. The 'keydown' event fires before the character is inserted — at that moment, the value hasn't changed yet (it's the previous value). It fires for any key press, including keys that don't change the value (Shift, Ctrl, Escape, arrows). Use 'input' when you care about the value changing (character counter, live search filtering). Use 'keydown' when you care about specific keys regardless of value (Enter to submit, Escape to close, arrow keys for navigation).

Write JavaScript that creates 3 list items dynamically. For each item: (1) createElement an <li> with textContent 'Item 1', 'Item 2', 'Item 3', (2) add a click event listener to each <li> that logs 'Clicked: ' + the item's textContent when clicked, (3) appendChild each <li> to the <ul> with id 'dynamic-list'.

Why do dynamically created elements (created with createElement after page load) need their event listeners attached at creation time? What alternative pattern handles this without attaching individual listeners?
questions.sample_answer: Event listeners must be attached after the element exists in memory. A statically written addEventListener in your script only runs once when the page loads — it can't see elements created later. So each dynamically created element needs its listener attached right after createElement, before or after appending. The alternative is event delegation: attach one listener to a parent element that already exists (like the <ul>), and use e.target inside the handler to determine which child was clicked. Since events bubble up from child to parent, the parent's listener catches clicks on all current and future children — no individual listeners needed.

Write JavaScript that: (1) adds a 'click' event listener to the button with id 'add-btn', (2) on each click, creates a new <div> with class 'notification' and textContent 'Notification ' + a counter (starting at 1), (3) creates a <button> with textContent 'Dismiss' that removes the notification div when clicked, (4) appends both to the element with id 'notification-area'. Counter increments with each click.
What is event delegation and why is it more efficient than adding individual event listeners to each child element? Give one practical scenario.
questions.sample_answer: Event delegation is the pattern of attaching a single event listener to a parent element instead of attaching separate listeners to each child. It works because of event bubbling — when a child is clicked, the event travels up through its ancestors, so the parent's listener fires. It's more efficient because: (1) one listener uses less memory than N listeners, (2) it automatically works for dynamically added children without re-attaching listeners, (3) it simplifies cleanup. Practical scenario: a to-do list where items are added and removed dynamically. Instead of attaching a delete listener to each new item's button, attach one listener to the <ul>. Check `e.target.classList.contains('delete-btn')` and remove `e.target.parentElement`. New items work immediately without extra code.
